dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s operating-model proposition with concrete examples of process mapping, multidisciplinary lawyer-technologist teams, technology-assisted review and alternative pricing. Although it does not address generative AI’s jagged capabilities or verification risks directly, it materially extends the synthesis by showing how workflow redesign and complementary organisational capabilities produced reported cost and time savings in legal service delivery.
qs: Of the practice group’s 71 people currently working full time, more than half (41) are “technologists”—individuals trained to understand the intersection between technology and law and who structure the framework of day-to-day operations and provide management and technological advice.
When e-discovery is necessary, eData deploys Legal Lean Sigma workflows and technology to streamline processes and reduce costs.

kp.k: Partners view efficiency demands as permanent
kp.d: The article reports that more than 90 percent of law firm partners in a 2014 Altman Weil survey regarded greater efficiency in legal services as a permanent market feature, with the same overwhelming percentage responding similarly in all four years the question had been asked.
qs: Indeed, more than 90 percent of law firm partners in a 2014 Altman Weil survey said they think greater efficiency in legal services is a permanent part of the market—and the same overwhelming percentage has said so for the past four years the survey has posed the question.

kp.k: Manufacturing methodologies reshape legal service processes
kp.d: The article describes firms borrowing Six Sigma and lean analysis from manufacturing to improve process design, reduce errors and remove nonessential work. Their combination, Legal Lean Sigma, targets eight categories of waste: defects, overproduction, waiting, nonutilized resources or talent, transportation, inventory, motion and excess processing.
qs: Six Sigma uses statistical analysis and a focus on client needs to improve process design and reduce error, while “lean” analysis reduces nonessential steps.
Lean Six Sigma combines the methodologies of Six Sigma and lean analysis, and the process has taken on the name Legal Lean Sigma in the legal services industry.

kp.k: Seyfarth combines client feedback, process maps and alternative pricing
kp.d: Drawing on partner Lisa J. Damon's December 2013/January 2014 Practical Law account, the article describes SeyfarthLean as integrating client interviews, standardized trial process maps and alternative pricing agreements. It also reports adoption of Six Sigma techniques by Baker & McKenzie, Freshfields Bruckhaus Deringer, Sullivan & Cromwell and DLA Piper.
qs: service model combines client interviews (called “voice of the client”), standardized trial process maps, and alternative pricing agreements.

Such project management is becoming increasingly common: the firms Baker & McKenzie, Freshfields Bruckhaus Deringer, Sullivan & Cromwell, and DLA Piper have all adopted Six Sigma techniques to improve legal processes.

kp.k: Clifford Chance reports substantial process-improvement savings
kp.d: The article cites Clifford Chance's 2014 white paper reporting 60 percent cost savings and production-time reductions of as much as 80 percent for post-litigation reference books, with one office producing 1,500 volumes annually. More broadly, the firm reported staff-time reductions of as much as half and time savings equivalent to about US $1.5 million in 2013. These are reported firm outcomes, rather than independent measurements presented by the article.
qs: it discovered cost savings of 60 percent, while the time required to produce each volume dropped by as much as 80 percent.
Since the firm produces 1,500 volumes each year in just one of its offices, such savings are not negligible.
Overall, Clifford Chance has found continuous improvement analyses can reduce staff time by as much as half.
In 2013, the firm saved time equivalent to about US $1.5 million by improving legal processes, and it has plans to train its entire staff in the methodology.

kp.k: Process understanding could change legal service valuation
kp.d: Clifford Chance's white paper suggests that deeper understanding of legal processes may fundamentally change how firms and clients value and price services. This is a proposed implication of continuous improvement, not an established market-wide outcome; the article also reports the firm's plan to train its entire staff in the methodology.
qs: The “deeper understanding” of legal processes that results from a careful continuous improvement analysis, the white paper notes, may “be a driver for a fundamental shift in the way in which law firms and their clients value and price legal services.”

kp.k: eData integrates lawyers and technologists within legal practice
kp.d: Morgan Lewis's eData practice, launched in 2004, combines partners, associates and technology staff across e-discovery, pre-litigation data management and information governance. The article reports 71 full-time personnel, including 41 technologists responsible for operational frameworks and management and technological advice, and states that all members are certified in Legal Lean Sigma. Metrics and project-specific resource selection underpin its delivery model.
qs: All are certified in Legal Lean Sigma methodologies.

Of the practice group’s 71 people currently working full time, more than half (41) are “technologists”—individuals trained to understand the intersection between technology and law and who structure the framework of day-to-day operations and provide management and technological advice.

Metrics closely track client discovery work, while the resources selected for each project are carefully tailored according to one of the practice group’s mottos: “Don’t offer a Cadillac when a bus token will do.”

kp.k: Information governance moves beyond keeping all organizational data
kp.d: Lead eData partner Stephanie A. “Tess” Blair contrasts organizations' tendency to keep everything 10 years earlier with their subsequent data overload. The practice develops lifecycle governance covering creation through disposal, intended to reduce unnecessary retention, clarify storage and access, support legal and business obligations, and facilitate discovery.
qs: Pre-litigation, eData works with clients to develop an information governance strategy, a holistic approach to data life-cycle management that addresses the creation, storage, access, search and retrieval, security, retention, and disposal of records throughout an organization.
Such a framework provides guidance about what to keep or discard, reducing unnecessary data retention while maximizing access to crucial knowledge resources within an organization.
Its goal is to turn information into an asset of an organization, rather than a liability.

kp.k: Technology-assisted review targets volume rather than cheaper labor
kp.d: Blair identifies overwhelming data volumes as the primary driver of e-discovery risk and cost. The article argues that outsourcing or offshoring can reduce document-review labor costs only so far without harming quality, whereas predictive coding and technology-assisted review reduce the volume requiring review and optimize reviewers' time. This describes technology-supported discovery, not an asserted replacement of lawyers or autonomous legal practice.
qs: According to Blair, the primary driver of e-discovery risk and cost is the often overwhelming volume of data created by litigation.

The labor costs of document review can only be reduced so much via outsourcing or offshoring before compromising quality of work, but eData’s expertise in predictive coding and technology-assisted review defensibly reduces the volume of data requiring review and streamlines the discovery process by optimizing each reviewer’s time.

kp.k: Client examples report discovery savings of 30–50 percent
kp.d: The article reports first-year savings of 30 percent after eData took over a high-tech company's litigation-portfolio discovery, and 50 percent savings for a pharmaceutical company following a tailored strategy replacing indiscriminate collection. eData's claim that it would further improve the former result through continuous process improvement is prospective, distinct from the reported savings.
qs: When the group took over discovery for a high-tech company’s litigation portfolio, the group delivered first-year cost savings of 30 percent—a number eData says it will continue to better over time with continuous process improvement.
Another pharmaceutical company saw cost savings of 50 percent when eData developed a tailored discovery strategy, replacing the inefficient “grab everything” strategy of its predecessor.

kp.k: Flat fees accompany savings guarantees and client-service recognition
kp.d: The article states that Morgan Lewis guarantees savings against clients' previous spending and that eData operates largely on flat fees while remaining among the firm's most successful divisions. It separately reports that BTI Consulting's 2014 corporate-counsel survey ranked Morgan Lewis fourth worldwide for client service. Blair emphasizes predictability, transparency and opportunities from integrated technology and legal thinking alongside cost savings.
qs: In fact, Morgan Lewis guarantees clients savings over their previous spending.
Its efforts seem to have paid off: the practice group operates largely on flat fee arrangements, yet is among the most successful divisions at the firm.
found Morgan Lewis ranked fourth in client service among law firms worldwide; eData in particular has been singled out among firms for its leadership in e-discovery.
But she also stressed the predictability, transparency, and even opportunities provided by integrating cutting-edge technology and first-rate legal thinking into data management and governance.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Predictive coding and technology-assisted review are presented as reducing the volume and cost of discovery work without sacrificing quality.
pts.d: The article attributes to Stephanie A. “Tess” Blair, lead partner of Morgan Lewis’ eData practice, the explanation that data volume drives discovery risk and cost and that outsourcing or offshoring alone has limits before quality suffers. It presents predictive coding and technology-assisted review as ways to reduce the documents requiring review and optimize reviewers’ time. The source discusses these specific technologies rather than generative AI or autonomous legal services. Its broader claims concern technology combined with Legal Lean Sigma workflows, not AI acting alone. The article also reports that eData guarantees savings, operates largely on flat fees, and is among the firm's most successful divisions.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of Blair’s practitioner account and client examples of savings from eData’s combined technology and process approach.
pts.d: The article reports first-year savings of 30 percent after eData took over a high-tech company's litigation discovery portfolio and savings of 50 percent for a pharmaceutical company following a tailored discovery strategy. These are examples of the practice group's overall service model; the article does not isolate the contribution of predictive coding or provide model-performance benchmarks, measured review accuracy, or a controlled comparison. Its claim that cost and quality can be reconciled rests on the described practice experience, rather than a separate quantitative quality assessment.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source describes an operating practice as of 2014 and reports a prediction of further savings through continuing process improvement.
pts.d: The article presents technology-assisted discovery as an existing capability, not a distant forecast. The high-tech client savings apply to the first year; eData predicts further improvement without specifying a deadline or magnitude. The benefits are described in the setting of high-volume discovery and depend on combining technology with tailored workflows, resource selection, and legal expertise. The source does not predict profession-wide displacement or a timetable for autonomous review.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Corporate clients gain lower discovery costs and greater predictability, while reviewers and technologists work within an integrated legal and technical delivery model.
pts.d: The affected market is corporate data management and litigation discovery, including high-tech and pharmaceutical clients. Human reviewers have a reduced document volume and more targeted use of their time; the article does not claim that they are eliminated. Morgan Lewis’ eData practice combines lawyers and technology specialists, reporting 41 technologists among 71 full-time personnel. Blair identifies predictability, transparency, and opportunities from integrating technology with legal thinking as client benefits beyond savings. The discussion concerns enterprise legal services rather than access to justice for underserved individuals.
